246.title: The other cheek (Matthew 5:38–42)
246.hook: no revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, go the second mile
246.howItsDone: The peace churches, such as Mennonites, Quakers and the Church of the Brethren, read this as a call to nonviolence; many other Christians apply it to personal insult and revenge, and practice it through forgiveness and generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nai, the plain Greek yes. Your line was yes means yes.

Somebody shoves you in line. Somebody posts something cruel about you. Somebody takes your parking space, then smirks. Everything in you wants to even the score, and maybe a little more than even, just so they learn. The next lines are hard ones: turn the other cheek, go the extra mile. People who've never opened a Bible use them. To hear them properly, start with the old rule he's quoting.
screen: `EVEN THE SCORE.` → `TURN THE OTHER CHEEK.` → `START WITH THE OLD RULE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth." That's from the law of Moses. It's often read as a limit on revenge rather than a command to take it: one eye for one eye, not a whole family for an eye. In Jewish tradition, the rabbis read it as fair compensation paid in court, not literal injury. Jesus goes further. "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Then three pictures. If someone sues you for your coat, give him your cloak too. And: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." Compel had a specific use: scholars say it meant soldiers and officials pressing locals into service, like carrying gear. It's the same Greek word Mark uses when the soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross. So picture a soldier of the occupying army ordering you to haul his pack. The order is one mile. Jesus says: go two. Readings differ. Some, like the scholar Walter Wink, argue that a slap on the right cheek was a backhanded insult, and turning the other cheek was a nonviolent way of standing your ground with dignity. Others read it more simply as refusing to retaliate at all. Churches differ, too: the peace churches say it rules out violence entirely; many other Christians say it governs personal revenge, not every use of force. What these readings share is the direction: break the cycle. Don't pay back.

segments.voice: Think of someone who asks more of you than you'd like: a demanding boss, a needy relative, a neighbor who always wants a favor. Picture doing what they usually ask, and then a little more, freely, before they ask; not because you have to, because you choose to. If it would put you in danger or let someone abuse you, that's not this, and if you pray, you can ask for a free heart.

247.title: Love your enemies (Matthew 5:43–48)
247.hook: pray for those who persecute you; the sun rises on the evil and the good
247.howItsDone: Some churches include prayers for enemies and those who wish harm in their regular intercessions, and Christians turn to this passage when facing conflict, war or personal injury.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compel: a soldier's order to carry his pack one mile, and Jesus saying go two. Your line was the second mile.

Tomorrow morning the sun will come up over your street. It will come through the window of the kindest person you know. And it will come through the window of the person you like least in the world, at exactly the same time, just as warm. The rain will fall on both your yards. The sky doesn't check anyone's record first. Jesus points to that ordinary fact, and builds a hard command on it.
screen: `THE SUN ON YOUR STREET.` → `THE PERSON YOU LIKE LEAST.` → `THE SKY DOESN'T CHECK.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy. The first half is from Leviticus: love thy neighbor as thyself. The second half isn't a verse anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, and nobody knows for sure where the saying came from. The book of Proverbs, in fact, says: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." Then, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." The word for love is agape, which Christian teachers often explain not as a warm feeling but as a choice to seek someone's good. You may never like your enemy. You can still want good for them. Why? "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." That's God's way, Jesus says: generous to everyone. If you love only those who love you, what reward is that? Even the tax collectors do the same. Then the chapter's last line: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. The Greek word, teleios, means whole, complete, grown up. Not flawless. Complete in love, the way the sun is complete, shining on every yard. Christians have tried to live this in extreme places: forgiving the people who killed their families, praying for their jailers. Jesus himself, Luke says, prayed from the cross for those crucifying him.

248.title: Not to be seen (Matthew 6:1–6)
248.hook: give, pray and fast in secret; your Father sees in secret
248.howItsDone: This passage is read in many churches on Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, when Christians take up quiet giving, prayer and fasting; some give anonymously and keep a private time of prayer each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, agape: choosing someone's good, even an enemy's. Your line was the sun shines on all.

Ever done something kind and felt the tiny itch to post about it? A donation, a volunteer shift, a good deed. Just a small photo, just so people know. That pull is nothing new. Jesus turns to three practices of his people's faith: giving to the poor, praying and fasting. He doesn't say don't do them. He assumes you will. He asks something sharper: who are you doing them for?
screen: `THE ITCH TO POST IT.` → `GIVING, PRAYING, FASTING.` → `WHO ARE YOU DOING IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Take heed, he says, that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them. Don't sound a trumpet when you give, the way the hypocrites do, to be praised. Nobody's sure anyone literally blew trumpets; it may be a vivid picture, like blowing your own horn. Then, in the King James Bible: "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Give so quietly that even you half forget it. Hypocrite is worth opening. In Greek, hupokrites meant a stage actor, someone who performed behind a mask. Jesus's point isn't about any one group. It's about anyone, in any faith or none, who performs goodness for an audience. Three times he says of them: they have their reward. Scholars point out that the Greek verb turns up on ancient receipts: paid in full. They wanted applause, they got it, and that's the whole payment. Then prayer: don't pray on street corners to be seen. Instead: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which is in secret shall reward thee openly." Closet here means an inner room, maybe a storeroom, the one room in a small house with a door. It doesn't mean praying together is wrong; Luke says Jesus went to the synagogue on the sabbath, as his custom was, and he taught his friends a prayer that begins our Father. It's about the audience. Fasting too: wash your face, look normal, let it be between you and God. Thy Father which is in secret, he says, sees it. On his telling, the quiet good isn't wasted.

249.title: Not many words (Matthew 6:7–8)
249.hook: your Father knows what you need before you ask
249.howItsDone: Christians pray both in set words and in their own words: Catholics and Orthodox often use repeated prayers like the rosary and the Jesus Prayer, and many Protestants favor short spontaneous prayers; across the churches, prayer is often described as turning toward God rather than informing him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hupokrites, an actor behind a mask, and a prayer behind a shut door. Your line was the father sees in secret.

Some people feel they can't pray because they don't know the right words. They've heard others pray beautifully, in long flowing sentences, and they freeze. Others pray the way people write emails to someone important: carefully, at length, explaining everything, just in case. Both are asking the same question: how much do I have to say to be heard? Right after shut the door and pray in secret, Jesus answers it.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `PRAYING LIKE A LONG EMAIL.` → `HOW MUCH DO I HAVE TO SAY?`

segments.voice: When you pray, he says, don't babble on, thinking you'll be heard because of your many words. The Greek verb is battalogeo. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and nobody knows exactly where it comes from. Some scholars think it's a sound word, like blah-blah-blah: batta-batta, heaping up syllables. Then the reason, in the King James Bible: "your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." That changes what prayer is for. You're not informing God. You're not filing a report. He already knows, Jesus says. So why pray at all? Christians have long asked that, and one common answer is that prayer isn't mainly for passing on information. It's for being with someone, like a friend who sits beside you in a hospital waiting room, not to pass on news, but to be with you. A fair question: what about repeating prayers? Christians read this verse in different ways. Catholics pray the rosary, Orthodox Christians repeat the Jesus Prayer, and they say the warning is against empty words, not repeated ones. After all, in Gethsemane, Mark says Jesus "went away, and prayed, and spake the same words." Some Protestant Christians hear the verse as a caution against praying by rote, and favor praying in their own words. Both agree on the heart: it's not the number of words that reaches God. The very next thing Jesus does is teach a short prayer, and that's tomorrow.

250.title: The prayer again (Matthew 6:9–15)
250.hook: the Lord's Prayer, set here in the middle of the sermon
250.howItsDone: Christians of every church pray the Lord's Prayer, in worship and at home; many pray it daily, and in most churches the congregation says it together, aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, battalogeo: babbling, heaping up empty words. Your line was he already knows.

A prayer you know by heart can slip right past you, like the words of a song you've sung a thousand times. Our Father. Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. You walked through it one line at a time back in the first weeks of this path, and you might know it by heart now. Today it turns up in a new place: not on its own, but set right in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount. Where it sits changes how it sounds.
screen: `A PRAYER KNOWN BY HEART.` → `BACK AT THE START OF THE PATH.` → `IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SERMON.`

segments.voice: Jesus has just said: don't pray to be seen, and don't babble. Then, in the King James Bible: "After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." After this manner: a pattern as well as a script. Short, plain, private enough to say behind a closed door, and yet it says our, not my. Many scholars notice that it sits near the very center of the sermon, as if the whole teaching turns around it. Everything before it, the Beatitudes, reconciling, loving enemies, is what it looks like when thy will be done on earth. For centuries, Western Christians prayed it in Latin, and its first two words, Pater noster, our Father, became a word of their own. Medieval prayer beads were called paternosters. A street near Saint Paul's Cathedral in London is still called Paternoster Row. There's even an open elevator, a chain of little rooms that never stops moving, called a paternoster, because it goes round and round like beads in praying hands. At the end, Matthew adds a line about forgiveness: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." It's the only line of the prayer Jesus explains. And the ending many people know, for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory? It's in the King James Bible, but not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew. It was likely added early for worship. Protestants usually pray it with the prayer; at Mass, Catholics say it a little later, after the priest's prayer.

251.title: Moths and rust (Matthew 6:19–21)
251.hook: where your treasure is, there your heart will be
251.howItsDone: Some Christians give a regular share of their income to church and to the poor, often following the biblical tithe, and think of generosity as laying up treasure in heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, paternoster: our Father, the first words of the Lord's Prayer. Your line was thy will be done.

Open a drawer you haven't opened in years. The sweater you loved has holes in it. The gadget that cost a week's pay won't turn on. The box of things you couldn't live without, you'd forgotten you had. Plenty of homes have a drawer like that. It's a little funny, and a little sobering: things you once treasured, quietly falling apart while you weren't looking. Jesus's listeners had drawers like that too, and he starts a new part of the sermon right there.
screen: `A DRAWER YOU HAVEN'T OPENED.` → `HOLES IN THE SWEATER.` → `THINGS YOU ONCE TREASURED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal." In his world, wealth could mean fine clothing, which moths could eat, and stored goods and metal, which could spoil and corrode. The Greek word translated rust literally means eating: anything that eats away, corrosion or vermin. And break through is, in Greek, dig through: a burglar who doesn't pick the lock, he digs through the wall. Nothing on earth is completely safe. Then the line that turns it all around: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Notice the order. You'd assume the heart leads and the money follows: I care about this, so I spend on it. Jesus says it also works the other way. Put your treasure somewhere, and your heart goes after it. That's hopeful: if you want to care more about something, you can start by giving to it. So what are treasures in heaven? Christians describe them as what moths can't eat: love given, mercy shown, the poor helped, time spent on what lasts. Read this way, Jesus isn't saying money doesn't matter. Money is more like a compass, showing where your heart is heading. Your bank statement, you could say, is a kind of spiritual diary.

Treasure. What moths and rust eat away on earth, and what Jesus says to store instead in heaven, where nothing can touch it. Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

252.title: The lamp of the body (Matthew 6:22–24)
252.hook: the eye is the lamp; you can't serve God and mammon
252.howItsDone: Christians often speak of stewardship, holding money as something entrusted by God, and some practice regular giving, simple living or fasting from spending as ways to keep money a servant rather than a master.

segments.voice: Yesterday, treasure: wherever it goes, the heart follows. Your line was where your treasure is. Today closes the week.

Try working for two bosses at once. One wants the report by noon; the other wants you at a meeting at noon. One says cut costs; the other says spend. Sooner or later you pick one, and the other one notices. Two jobs, or two households with different rules, work the same way. Jesus has two pictures for it: a lamp, and a servant with two masters.
screen: `TWO BOSSES AT ONCE.` → `SOONER OR LATER, YOU PICK ONE.` → `A LAMP, AND TWO MASTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the lamp. In the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light." Single translates a Greek word that can mean simple, undivided, and also generous. In Jewish idiom, a good eye meant a generous person, and an evil eye a stingy one. Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he gives his bread to the poor. So a single eye looks at the world openly and generously, and the whole person fills with light. A grasping eye darkens everything. Then the second picture: "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Serve here means serve as a slave, not a part-time job, and a slave can't belong fully to two owners. Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth or property, the stuff you own and rely on. Some scholars think it comes from a root meaning that in which you trust, though nobody is sure. It wasn't the name of a god; medieval writers later turned Mammon into a demon, and the poet Milton put him in Paradise Lost. But Jesus uses it almost like a person, a rival master, because that's how money can act: it makes demands, it promises safety, it asks for your time and your worry. Look back at this week: the other cheek, love for enemies, giving in secret, few words, our Father, moths and rust, and now one master. Each asks: who, finally, do you belong to?
screen: `THE EYE IS THE LAMP.` · `SINGLE: UNDIVIDED, GENEROUS.` · `NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.` · `MAMMON: WEALTH YOU TRUST.` · then, large: `YE CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.`

segments.voice: Think back over today: where did your eyes keep landing? Price tags, other people's things, your balance, a face you love; no verdict, just notice. Then picture your eye as a lamp and ask what today would look like through a generous eye, and if you pray, ask for a single eye.
Mammon. Aramaic for wealth, the things you own and trust; Jesus names it as a rival master. You can't serve both.
Your line: one master. A single eye fills the whole body with light. And that's a week.
